recipe.history:
Curry — the Western term that encompasses an enormously diverse range of spiced dishes from South and Southeast Asia — has no single origin but rather a complex, layered history rooted primarily in the Indian subcontinent, where spiced gravies and dry-spiced preparations have been part of cooking for at least four thousand years. The word curry itself is likely derived from the Tamil word kari, meaning sauce, and was applied by Portuguese and later British colonizers to a vast range of Indian dishes they grouped under a single convenient label. Red curry, the specific tradition drawn upon in this recipe, originates in Thai cuisine, where dried red chilies — varieties like prik haeng and prik chee fa — are ground with lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime zest, shrimp paste, shallots, and garlic into a paste of extraordinary aromatic complexity. Thai red curry paste is fundamentally different from Indian curry powder: it is a fresh paste of pounded aromatics rather than a dry blend, and it delivers heat, fragrance, and depth simultaneously.

Curry's entrance into American cooking came through waves of immigration — South Asian, Southeast Asian, and Caribbean communities all brought spiced cooking traditions that began to influence mainstream American taste from the 1970s onward. Thai restaurants proliferated in American cities from the 1980s, and Thai red curry in particular became one of the most recognized and beloved international flavors in American cooking. Using red curry as the flavor base for a burger aioli — blending the paste into a mayonnaise base to create a creamy, spicy, aromatic sauce — and for a set of deeply caramelized onions seasoned with curry powder and coconut sugar is a form of American culinary translation: taking a foreign flavor tradition and routing it through the most American of food formats. The result is a burger that smells like a Thai kitchen and eats like an American one.

I discovered the red curry aioli by accident, as the best sauces often arrive. I had leftover Thai red curry paste in the refrigerator after making a batch of curry that had come out more paste-forward than I wanted, and I was looking at a bowl of freshly made mayonnaise. I stirred a spoonful of the paste into the mayo on a whim, tasted it on a piece of bread, and immediately understood that I had made something that belonged on a burger. The warmth of the chilies, the floral quality of the lemongrass and lime, and the savory depth of the shrimp paste transformed the mayonnaise from a condiment into a statement. The curry-spiced caramelized onions came next, built by the logic of following one good idea with another: if the aioli would be spiced, the onions should be too, but cooked long and slow so the curry became caramel-sweet and round rather than sharp.

Medium rare is the temperature of respect for flavor complexity. A burger built around a sauce as aromatic and layered as red curry aioli needs the richness and weight of a properly pink, fat-saturated patty to serve as its platform. A well-done patty is too dry and one-dimensional to support such a complex condiment — the patty becomes merely a vehicle and the burger becomes unbalanced. At 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, the medium-rare beef contributes its own deep, iron-rich, fatty flavor to the conversation, matching the intensity of the curry components without being drowned by them. Medium rare is not the easiest thing to cook consistently, but it is the temperature at which the beef becomes a genuine partner to its toppings rather than a background player.
ingredients: 1/4 cup coconut oil, melted and cooled
3 tbsp Thai red curry paste (store-bought or homemade)
4 oz paneer, cut into 1/4-inch slices and pan-fried until golden
instructions: 1. Make the naan-style buns: Bloom yeast in warm water with sugar for 5 minutes. Combine flour and salt in a bowl. Add yeast mixture, yogurt, and oil; mix until a soft dough forms. Knead 8 minutes until smooth. Cover and rise 1 hour.
2. Divide dough into 6 equal balls. Roll each into an oval shape about 5 inches across and 1/2 inch thick. Place on parchment-lined baking sheet; proof 20 minutes.

3. Heat a heavy cast-iron skillet over high heat. Cook naan buns dry, one at a time, pressing gently with a spatula, 2–3 minutes per side until charred spots form and buns puff slightly. Brush immediately with melted butter and scatter nigella seeds. Stack and keep warm.

4. Make the curry-spiced caramelized onions: Melt butter in a heavy skillet over medium-low heat. Add onions and a pinch of salt. Cook slowly 40–50 minutes, stirring frequently, until deep golden and jammy. Add coconut sugar, curry powder, cumin, turmeric, and cayenne; stir and cook 3 minutes. Deglaze with cider vinegar; cook until syrupy. Season.

5. Make the red curry aioli: Whisk egg yolks and Dijon together. Stream in neutral oil and then coconut oil very slowly, whisking constantly, until thick and emulsified. Whisk in curry paste, lime juice, fish sauce, honey, and garlic paste. Season with salt. Refrigerate.
6. Pan-fry paneer: Heat 1 tbsp neutral oil in a skillet over medium-high heat. Fry paneer slices 2–3 minutes per side until golden and crisp. Season with a pinch of salt. Set aside.
7. Form the patties: Combine ground chuck with salt, pepper, coriander, and cumin. Divide into 4 portions (8 oz each). Shape into 4.5-inch patties with a center dimple. Refrigerate 20 minutes.

8. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat with thin film of neutral oil. Cook patties undisturbed 3–4 minutes. Flip; top each with golden paneer slices. Cook 2–3 more minutes. Target 130–135°F internal temperature for medium rare. Remove, tent with foil, rest 3 minutes.
9. Toss cucumber with lime juice and a pinch of salt.
10. Halve naan buns. Briefly toast cut sides in butter in skillet, 60 seconds.

11. Assemble: Spread red curry aioli generously on both cut sides of the naan bun. Place baby spinach on the bottom. Add curry-spiced caramelized onions. Set the patty with paneer on top. Add cucumber slices and fresh cilantro. Finish with flaky sea salt. Crown with the top bun.
